text: Not really the same. Film is closer to gaming than music, but there are still too many differences to copy another industry’s model. For example, music pays artists per stream, but film does not. That difference comes down to how contracts have traditionally worked. Music contracts were based on sales numbers, with labels taking on little risk, so per-stream payments made sense. Film usually works with lump-sum contracts where the studio fronts the costs and hopes to earn it back later. Games are closer to film, but you don't have platforms vying to buy your product towards the end of production. Typically games have target platforms set near the beginning of production. More often than not the publisher of a game dictates the target platforms themselves, rather than shopping their product to various platforms to pick up like in film.

text: It's always a balance between sales potential and financial stability for the devs. It's easy to say "oh we could have made more !" when the game already sold well. I know a studio owner that went through a gamepass deal. His take on it was that it didn't maximize potential revenue but it absolutely guaranteed that he had paid back his production costs day one. Every sale was pure profit, even though he may have done less of them overall. The reality is that plenty, if not a majority of good games bomb. And that's the kind of shit that kills a studio. Whatever people might think, studio execs (especially small/medium sized ones) are passionate and want to keep going to make their next game. For a good number of them having the guarantee that you will not close your shop down if the game doesn't do well is a fantastic deal. Things like Hollowknight or Expedition 33 are the game dev equivalent of winning the powerball. It should absolutely not be considered as achievable by even a minority of studios.
